title: Arc Length and Curvature
lead: The arc length of a curve $\kvecr(t)$ is the integral of its speed $\|\kvecrprime(t)\|$; measured from a starting point it becomes the arc-length function and a new parameter. Curvature measures how sharply the curve turns, as the rate at which its unit tangent turns per unit of length, and the principal unit normal and binormal vectors complete a frame that rides along the curve.
objectives: Determine the length of a particle’s path in space by using the arc-length function.
Explain the meaning of the curvature of a curve in space and state its formula.
Describe the meaning of the normal and binormal vectors of a curve in space.
summary_html:
• The arc-length function for a vector-valued function is calculated using the integral formula $\ks(t)=\int_a^{t}\| \kvecrprime(u)\| \;du .$ This formula is valid in both two and three dimensions.
  • The curvature of a curve at a point in either two or three dimensions is defined to be the curvature of the inscribed circle at that point. The arc-length parameterization is used in the definition of curvature.
  • There are several different formulas for curvature. The curvature of a circle is equal to the reciprocal of its radius.
  • The principal unit normal vector at t is defined to be $$\kvecN(t)=\frac{\kvecTprime(t)}{\| \kvecTprime(t)\|}.$$
  • The binormal vector at t is defined as $\kvecB(t)=\kvecT(t)\;\times \;\kvecN(t),$ where $\kvecT(t)$ is the unit tangent vector.
  • The Frenet frame of reference is formed by the unit tangent vector, the principal unit normal vector, and the binormal vector.
  • The osculating circle is tangent to a curve at a point and has the same curvature as the tangent curve at that point.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the arc length of the parameterized curve

$$\textbf{r}(t)=\langle 2t^{2}+1,2t^{2}-1,t^{3}\rangle ,0\le t\le 3.$$

Find the arc-length function for the helix

$$\textbf{r}(t)=\langle 3\;\cos t,3\;\sin t,4t\rangle ,t\ge 0.$$

Then, use the relationship between the arc length and the parameter t to find an arc-length parameterization of $\textbf{r}(t).$

answer.solution: $s=5t,$ or $t=s/5.$ Substituting this into $\textbf{r}(t)=\langle 3\;\cos t,3\;\sin t,4t\rangle$ gives $\textbf{r}(s)=\langle 3\;\cos (\frac{s}{5}),\;3\;\sin (\frac{s}{5}),\frac{4s}{5}\rangle ,s\ge 0.$
answer.hint: Start by finding the arc-length function.

exercises.prompt:
The surface of a large cup is formed by revolving the graph of the function $y=0.25x^{1.6}$ from $x=0$ to $x=5$ about the y-axis (measured in centimeters).

Find the curvature $\kappa$ of the generating curve as a function of x.

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The curvature of a circle of radius $r$ is constant everywhere. Furthermore, the curvature is equal to $1/r.$

answer.solution: True. The circle of radius $r$ is $\mathbf{r}(t)=r\cos t\,\mathbf{i}+r\sin t\,\mathbf{j},$ with $\mathbf{r}\'(t)=-r\sin t\,\mathbf{i}+r\cos t\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\|\mathbf{r}\'(t)\|=r.$ Then $\mathbf{T}(t)=-\sin t\,\mathbf{i}+\cos t\,\mathbf{j},$ $\mathbf{T}\'(t)=-\cos t\,\mathbf{i}-\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\|\mathbf{T}\'(t)\|=1,$ so $\kappa=\frac{\|\mathbf{T}\'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf{r}\'(t)\|}=\frac{1}{r}$ for every $t$: the same at every point of the circle, and equal to the reciprocal of the radius.

footnotes.html: As $t$ runs from $0$ to $h$ the helix completes $N$ turns, so $h$ is the height of the whole helix; two consecutive turns are $\frac{h}{N}$ apart, and the two agree only when $N=1.$

Equation 13.17 is the curvature of a graph; the binormal vector is Equation 13.19, $\mathbf{B}(t)=\mathbf{T}(t)\times\mathbf{N}(t),$ which the calculation uses. Its $\mathbf{k}$-component is printed $\frac{-15-15t^{2}}{25(t^{2}+1)}$; the determinant gives $\frac{15+15t^{2}}{25(t^{2}+1)},$ as the next line uses, and $\mathbf{B}(t)=\frac{4}{5}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{5}\mathbf{k}.$

Here $\mathbf{r}'(t)=(2t-3)\,\mathbf{i}+4\,\mathbf{j},$ so $\mathbf{r}'(2)=\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j},$ and the printed $\mathbf{N}(2)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$ is not orthogonal to it. Since $\mathbf{r}''(t)=2\,\mathbf{i}$ turns the curve clockwise, $\mathbf{N}(2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}(4\,\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}).$ The hint’s Equation 13.13 is the arc-length function; $\mathbf{N}$ is Equation 13.18.
The caption’s “the point where $t=1$” is the point where $x=1.$
